text.title: Business Model Research Core Rules
text.summary: Testable rules grounding the Business Model Research methodology. Every rule pairs a binary check with sourced rationale, plus the universal skip-this-methodology gate. Folds in the former canvas/revenue and unit-economics files: Nine-block Business Model Canvas with Hard/Soft cell tagging and five revenue archetypes with variant tables and best-fit signals. CAC/LTV/payback formulas, P10/P50/P90 scenario model, churn floor rules, and five stress tests that define model viability.

rule.statement: Populate all 9 Canvas blocks before naming any price; tag each cell Hard (sourced from a public filing, pricing page, or comparable company) or Soft (founder estimate).
rule.rationale: Agents skip the Canvas and produce unit economics without understanding the cost structure. Hard/Soft tagging makes the assumptions ledger auditable and enables future re-runs to diff what changed. The nine blocks are listed in the Canvas blocks section below.

rule.statement: Shortlist exactly 2 of the 5 revenue archetypes that fit the value chain; reject the others on record with a one-line reason before running unit economics.
rule.rationale: LLMs default to SaaS subscription whenever the product is digital. Forcing an explicit rejection of the other four archetypes surfaces assumptions that would otherwise remain implicit. The five archetypes are listed in the Revenue archetypes section below.

rule.statement: Always compute LTV with a lifetime cap of 60 months — the formula 1/churn explodes at low churn rates and produces fantasy LTVs.
rule.rationale: 1% monthly churn implies 100-month (8.3 year) average lifetime. SaaS products rarely sustain customers that long. Cap at 60 months unless backed by a 10-K showing 5-year cohorts.

rule.statement: Run unit economics in three scenarios (P10 pessimistic, P50 base, P90 optimistic) before writing any verdict; the P10 verdict is the only one that matters for runway and hiring decisions.
rule.rationale: Single-point LTV:CAC hides the distribution. Investors and operators need to know if the model survives a bad quarter (P10), not just a median one. Refusing to average ranges is a hard rule.

rule.statement: The model passes only if it survives all five stress tests at P50 and does not go below 1:1 LTV:CAC at P10. The five are Scale, Competition, Churn, CAC and Time-to-profit, defined in the Five stress tests section below.
rule.rationale: A model that passes only 4 of 5 tests at P50 has a known failure mode that will materialize as the business scales. Documenting the failure mode is more valuable than optimistic forecasting.

rule.statement: Refuse to compute LTV with monthly churn below 1% unless backed by a public 10-K — sub-1% churn is a unicorn claim requiring evidence.
rule.rationale: Agents accept 0.5%/month churn from a blog post; LTV explodes 5x and the model looks viable when it is not. Baremetrics benchmarks show median SaaS monthly churn at 2-4%.

rule.statement: Model churn as cohort-variable, not flat — month-1 churn is 3-10x month-12 churn. Flat churn assumptions understate early-cohort losses.
rule.rationale: New users churn at much higher rates than retained users. A flat 3%/month model dramatically underestimates first-month losses and overestimates LTV.

rule.statement: Apply this methodology only if all entries in `## Applies If` hold and none of `## Skip If` triggers; otherwise abort and route to the correct methodology.

rationale.source: F-066 spec — decision tree minimum form

rule.rationale: A misrouted methodology produces wrong-shape output; the explicit skip rule is the universal default branch from the decision tree.

list.item: Customer Segments: who are the paying users? primary + secondary
Value Propositions: what value is delivered to each segment?
Channels: awareness, evaluation, purchase, delivery, after-sales
Customer Relationships: self-serve / assisted / automated; retention mechanisms
Revenue Streams: model type, price, estimated % of total revenue
Key Resources: physical, intellectual, human, financial
Key Activities: the 3 most critical activities for delivering value
Key Partners: what they provide, what they get in return
Cost Structure: fixed vs variable; cost-driven vs value-driven orientation
Subscription/SaaS: flat rate, tiered, per-seat, usage-based, freemium — best for ongoing value delivery, sticky products. Key metrics: MRR, churn, LTV, CAC.
One-time purchase: digital product, software license, physical product — best for discrete value and impulse buys. Key metrics: units sold, revenue per product, repeat purchase rate.
Transaction-based: percentage cut, flat fee per transaction, hybrid — best for marketplaces, payments, brokerage. Key metrics: GMV, take rate, transaction volume.
Advertising: display, sponsored, affiliate — best for high-traffic content platforms. Key metrics: DAU, CPM, CTR, ad inventory fill rate.
Marketplace/Commission: service, product, lead generation — best for matching problems with network effects. Key metrics: GMV, take rate, liquidity.
CAC = total marketing + sales spend / new customers acquired (use paid CAC for LTV:CAC, not blended)
LTV = ARPU * gross_margin * min(1/churn, 60 months)
LTV:CAC ratio target: 3:1 or higher. Below 1:1 = burning cash on acquisition. Below 3:1 = marginal at scale.
Payback period = CAC / (ARPU * gross_margin). Target: <12 months. >24 months requires exceptional retention evidence.
Scale: does unit economics hold at 10x, 100x customers? (Watch: marginal infrastructure costs, support load)
Competition: what if prices drop 50%? (Check: can gross margin absorb a 50% ARPU cut?)
Churn: what if monthly churn doubles? (Run: P10 with churn * 2 applied)
CAC: what if acquisition costs rise 3x? (Check: channel saturation, Apple ATT, cookie deprecation)
Time: how long until profitable at P50? (Calculate: break-even customer count = fixed costs / contribution margin)
